sections.heading: Coming to you honestly
sections.text: God, thank you that I can come near to you. I don’t want to pretend I am better than I am. I have sinned, and I am guilty before you. I confess the wrong in me plainly, and I ask you, because of your mercy, to forgive me.
theological_themes: Approaching God with both confidence and honesty
Confession of sin without excuse
Asking God for mercy and forgiveness

scripture_references.connection: John holds together honest confession and confidence in God’s forgiveness. This supports the prayer’s refusal to deny guilt while still coming to God for cleansing.
Because Christ is the great high priest, believers may draw near to God for mercy and help. This grounds the prayer’s confidence to approach God even while aware of sin.

sections.heading: Choosing you over sin’s easier path
sections.text: Please help me make the better choice, even when it costs me. If following you brings hardship, let me choose that rather than enjoy sin for a little while and lose what matters most. Train my heart to believe that obedience with you is better than comfort without you.
theological_themes: Preferring faithfulness to temporary sinful pleasure
Endurance in hardship for God’s sake
Faith that values God’s promises above immediate ease

scripture_references.connection: Moses is presented as choosing mistreatment with God’s people over the passing pleasures of sin because he valued God’s reward more. This is the direct biblical pattern behind the prayer’s request.

Jesus teaches that following him may involve self-denial and loss, but gaining the world is no bargain if the soul is lost. This supports the prayer’s desire to choose costly obedience over destructive pleasure.

sections.heading: Keeping me close and changing me deeply
sections.text: Keep me under your care and direction. Help me hold tightly to the promises that bind me to you in Christ. Let my faith not be only something I say I believe, but something that cleanses me, humbles me, dignifies me, and makes me gentle. Make me more compassionate, more loving, more tender toward weakness, and more courteous in the way I treat people.
theological_themes: God’s guiding and preserving care
Confidence in God’s covenant promises in Christ
Sanctification that changes character and relationships
Christian love expressed in compassion and gentleness

scripture_references.connection: The psalm portrays the Lord as the shepherd who guides, restores, and protects his people. It supports the prayer’s desire to live under God’s directing and guarding care.
Peter connects God’s promises and power with growth in godly qualities such as self-control, affection, and love. This fits the prayer’s longing for professed faith to have a real purifying effect.
Paul calls God’s chosen people to put on compassion, kindness, humility, meekness, patience, and love. This passage grounds the prayer’s request for a softer, more loving character.

sections.heading: Offering myself for your use
sections.text: Father, let me count it an honor to be useful to you. I don’t want to bury what you have given me or spend it only on myself. Make me ready for the opportunities you put in front of me, and help me offer my abilities, time, and strength for your service.
theological_themes: Service as a privilege from God
Stewardship of gifts and abilities
Readiness for usefulness in ordinary opportunities

scripture_references.connection: Peter teaches that each believer has received gifts to steward for the good of others and the glory of God. This supports the prayer’s offering of talents for God’s service.
Paul uses the image of a vessel made useful and ready for honorable purposes. This fits the prayer’s desire to be an instrument in God’s hands, prepared for useful work.

sections.heading: Trusting your wise refusals
sections.text: You have done what is good for me, even when I did not understand it. You have remembered me, set your kindness on me, and given me more than I deserve. Not every desire of mine has been satisfied, but I believe your love has sometimes protected me by saying no. You have kept back things that would have harmed me if I had received them.
theological_themes: God’s providence over both gifts and denials
Trusting God’s wisdom when desires are not granted
God’s love as protective, not merely indulgent

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that God works all things for good for those who love him. This gives biblical ground for trusting that even denied desires may be part of God’s wise care.
The psalm says the Lord gives what is good and does not withhold good from those who walk uprightly. This supports the prayer’s belief that God’s refusals are not neglect but wise love.

sections.heading: Praising you for discipline, comfort, and mercy
sections.text: My troubles have been less than my sins deserve. When you have corrected me, it has not been cruel; it has been for my good. And when I have humbled myself under your hand, you have also lifted the weight, wiped away my tears, and brought peace back to my grieving heart. Everything you do for me is right, wise, and complete. I praise you.
theological_themes: God’s merciful restraint in affliction
Fatherly discipline for holiness and good
God’s comfort in sorrow
Praise for the perfection of God’s works

scripture_references.connection: Jeremiah recognizes that God’s people are not consumed because of his steadfast love and mercy. This supports the prayer’s confession that troubles have been less than sins deserve.
Hebrews explains divine discipline as the loving correction of a Father, intended to produce holiness and peaceable fruit. This grounds the prayer’s view of chastening as painful but profitable.
Paul praises God as the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts his people in affliction. This supports the prayer’s gratitude for tears wiped away and peace restored.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original interprets trials and denied desires as expressions of God’s loving providence and fatherly discipline. This is biblically grounded, but pastorally sensitive because not every hardship should be simplistically explained as a specific punishment or correction.

The phrase about choosing affliction rather than the pleasures of sin is rooted in Hebrews 11’s account of Moses. I preserved the stark contrast without implying that suffering is good in itself; the good is faithfulness to God over sin.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered the 'sure covenant' as the promises that bind the believer to God in Christ, since the prayer is asking for stronger grasp of God’s covenantal commitment rather than introducing a technical covenant-theology discussion.

I interpreted the 'purifying, dignifying, softening influence of the religion I profess' as the lived effect of Christian faith: cleansing from sin, humility, restored dignity in God’s grace, gentleness, compassion, and love.

I adapted 'when I have kissed the rod it has fallen from thy hands' as humbling oneself under God’s discipline and finding that God lifts the weight. This preserves the original’s image of submitted correction followed by mercy without carrying over an obscure idiom.
